definition: A refinement of scaling laws showing that many large language models had been undertrained relative to their size, and that model size and training tokens should scale roughly equally.
details: The Chinchilla paper argued that, for a fixed compute budget, better performance is achieved by training a smaller model on more data than by training a larger model on less data, reshaping how subsequent LLMs were trained.
story: Imagine a factory floor where each workstation can glance at every other workstation before doing its part. It is the blueprint that makes everything else possible. At the bottom of every machine is a design — the shape of it, and how its pieces talk to each other. Structure decides what the model can even express — the blueprint before the bricks. That blueprint is Chinchilla Scaling.
